title: Network Performance: Latency, Bandwidth, and Throughput

questions.prompt: Match each performance term to its definition.

pairs.right: Maximum capacity a link could carry
Delay for data to travel / round-trip

questions.explanation: Bandwidth is capacity, throughput is achieved rate, latency is delay, and jitter is how much the delay varies.

questions.prompt: Why can't buying more bandwidth reduce latency?

options.text: Latency is set mainly by distance and hops, not by capacity
Bandwidth and latency are the same thing
Latency only depends on the file size

questions.explanation: RTT is dominated by physical distance and the number of hops; adding capacity doesn't shorten how long data takes to travel the path.

questions.prompt: Bandwidth multiplied by RTT gives the amount of data that must be in flight to fill a link — the bandwidth-____ product.
questions.explanation: The bandwidth-delay product (bandwidth × RTT) is the in-flight data needed to saturate a link; too-small windows waste capacity.

questions.prompt: A 100 Mb/s link transfers data at roughly how many megabytes per second (before overhead)?
questions.explanation: Since 1 byte = 8 bits, 100 megabits/s ÷ 8 ≈ 12.5 megabytes/s, and that's before protocol overhead.

questions.prompt: Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: TCP treats packet loss as congestion and slows down
Bufferbloat adds latency under load from oversized buffers
Many web page loads are latency-bound due to multiple round trips
Throughput can exceed the link's bandwidth

questions.explanation: Loss triggers congestion control, bufferbloat spikes latency, and page loads are often latency-bound. Throughput can never exceed bandwidth.

questions.prompt: Order the round trips (roughly) before content on a cold HTTPS page load from a distant server.
questions.explanation: A cold load resolves DNS, completes the TCP handshake, then the TLS handshake, then the request — several RTTs before the first byte.
